# STEP 01 — Load the Data

Read the CSV file into R. Keep the full dataset because later steps need the sample columns.

```{r}
CD_data_microbiom_essential <- read.csv("C:/Users/R DM/OneDrive/Desktop/Bactiriom data analysis/CD_data_microbiom_essential.csv")
```

# STEP 02 — Rename the Microorganism Column

Rename the column `X` to `micro-organism`, if the imported file contains a column named `X`.

```{r}
colnames(CD_data_microbiom_essential)[colnames(CD_data_microbiom_essential) == "X"] <- "micro-organism"
```

# Question 1: How widespread is each microorganism within CD patient samples?

The `prevalence` column describes how widespread each microorganism is across the CD samples.

## STEP 03 — Sort by Prevalence

Sort microorganisms from the highest prevalence to the lowest.

```{r}
sorted_data <- CD_data_microbiom_essential[order(CD_data_microbiom_essential$prevalence, decreasing = TRUE), ]

par(mar = c(5, 12, 4, 2))

barplot(
  rev(sorted_data$prevalence),
  names.arg = rev(sorted_data$`micro-organism`),
  horiz = TRUE,
  las = 1,
  col = "steelblue",
  cex.names = 0.7,
  xlab = "Prevalence (%)",
  main = "Prevalence Bar Plot of Micro-organisms"
)
```

- `order(..., decreasing = TRUE)` sorts rows by prevalence, highest first.
- `par(mar = ...)` adjusts the plot margins to make room for microorganism names.
- `barplot(...)` creates the horizontal bar plot.

## STEP 04 — Create a ggplot2 Bar Plot

Create a second prevalence plot using `ggplot2`.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(CD_data_microbiom_essential, aes(x = reorder(`micro-organism`, -prevalence), y = prevalence)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    x = "Micro-organism",
    y = "Prevalence (%)",
    title = "Prevalence Bar Plot of Micro-organisms"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

- `reorder(..., -prevalence)` orders microorganisms by decreasing prevalence.
- `geom_col()` draws bars using the prevalence values.
- `coord_flip()` makes the bars horizontal.
- `labs()` sets the labels and title.

# STEP 05 — Convert Sample Columns to Long Format

Reshape the sample columns into two columns: `sample` and `abundance`. The first two columns (`micro-organism` and `prevalence`) are kept as identifier columns.

```{r}
library(tidyr)

df_long_2 <- pivot_longer(
  CD_data_microbiom_essential,
  cols = 3:ncol(CD_data_microbiom_essential),
  names_to = "sample",
  values_to = "abundance"
)

df_long_2$prevalence <- NULL
```

- `pivot_longer()` converts the sample columns into rows.
- `names_to = "sample"` stores sample names.
- `values_to = "abundance"` stores abundance values.
- `df_long_2$prevalence <- NULL` removes the prevalence column from the long-format table.

# Question 2: Which species shows the greatest variation in abundance among the CD samples?

## STEP 06 — Plot Abundance Values

Plot the abundance values for the first 750 rows of the long-format table.

```{r}
n_rows <- min(750, nrow(df_long_2))

ggplot(df_long_2[1:n_rows, ], aes(x = seq_len(n_rows), y = abundance)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 1.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Scatter Plot of Abundance",
    x = "Observation",
    y = "Abundance"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

- `min(750, nrow(df_long_2))` avoids asking for more rows than the dataset contains.
- `geom_point()` plots abundance observations.

## STEP 07 — Compare Abundance Across Microorganisms

Select up to 750 samples and show a separate panel for each microorganism.

```{r}
samples_750 <- unique(df_long_2$sample)[seq_len(min(750, length(unique(df_long_2$sample))))]
df_sub <- df_long_2[df_long_2$sample %in% samples_750, ]

ggplot(df_sub, aes(x = sample, y = abundance)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ `micro-organism`, scales = "free_y") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank()
  )
```

- `samples_750` selects up to 750 distinct sample names.
- `facet_wrap()` creates a separate panel for each microorganism.
- `scales = "free_y"` allows each microorganism panel to use its own y-axis scale.

# Question 3: What is the distribution pattern of relative abundance for each species across CD patient samples?

## STEP 08 — Create Boxplots

Use the first 21 unique samples to display the distribution of abundance for each microorganism.

```{r}
samples_21 <- unique(df_long_2$sample)[seq_len(min(21, length(unique(df_long_2$sample))))]
df_sub <- df_long_2[df_long_2$sample %in% samples_21, ]

ggplot(df_sub, aes(x = `micro-organism`, y = abundance)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue", color = "darkblue", outlier.size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ `micro-organism`, scales = "free") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 6, face = "bold")
  )
```

- `geom_boxplot()` summarizes the distribution, including the median and quartiles.
- `facet_wrap()` creates a separate panel for each microorganism.

## STEP 09 — Create Violin Plots

A violin plot shows the shape of the abundance distribution for each microorganism.

```{r}
samples_21 <- unique(df_long_2$sample)[seq_len(min(21, length(unique(df_long_2$sample))))]
df_sub <- df_long_2[df_long_2$sample %in% samples_21, ]

ggplot(df_sub, aes(x = `micro-organism`, y = abundance)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "lightblue", color = "darkblue", trim = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ `micro-organism`, scales = "free") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 6, face = "bold")
  )
```

- `geom_violin()` displays the distribution density.
- `trim = FALSE` keeps the violin tails from being trimmed to the observed range.

# Question 4: Are the most widespread species the same as those with the highest abundance?

**Null Hypothesis (H₀):** There is no significant monotonic correlation between species prevalence and median relative abundance in CD samples.

**Alternative Hypothesis (H₁):** There is a significant monotonic correlation between species prevalence and median relative abundance in CD samples.

## STEP 10 — Calculate Median Abundance

Calculate the median abundance across the sample columns for each microorganism. The full dataset must still contain the sample columns for this step.

```{r}
CD_data_microbiom_essential$Median_Abundance <- apply(
  CD_data_microbiom_essential[, 3:ncol(CD_data_microbiom_essential)],
  1,
  median,
  na.rm = TRUE
)
```

- `[, 3:ncol(...)]` selects the sample columns.
- `apply(..., 1, median)` calculates the median across each row.
- `na.rm = TRUE` ignores missing values when calculating the median.

## STEP 11 — Test the Spearman Correlation

Test whether prevalence and median abundance are monotonically associated.

```{r}
cor.test(
  CD_data_microbiom_essential$prevalence,
  CD_data_microbiom_essential$Median_Abundance,
  method = "spearman",
  exact = FALSE
)
```

- `cor.test()` performs a statistical correlation test.
- `method = "spearman"` uses Spearman's rank correlation.
- `exact = FALSE` avoids exact p-value calculation, which can be unsuitable when ties occur.

## STEP 12 — Plot and Annotate the Correlation

Plot prevalence against median abundance, add a linear trend line, and display Spearman's rho.

```{r}
plot(
  x = CD_data_microbiom_essential$prevalence,
  y = CD_data_microbiom_essential$Median_Abundance,
  main = "Spearman Correlation: Prevalence vs Median Abundance",
  xlab = "Prevalence (%)",
  ylab = "Median Relative Abundance",
  pch = 19,
  col = "steelblue",
  cex = 1.2
)

abline(
  lm(Median_Abundance ~ prevalence, data = CD_data_microbiom_essential),
  col = "darkred",
  lwd = 2
)

cor_val <- cor(
  CD_data_microbiom_essential$prevalence,
  CD_data_microbiom_essential$Median_Abundance,
  method = "spearman",
  use = "complete.obs"
)

mtext(
  text = paste("Spearman Rho =", round(cor_val, 3)),
  side = 3,
  line = 0.5,
  col = "darkblue",
  cex = 0.9
)
```

- `plot()` creates the scatter plot.
- `abline(lm(...))` adds a linear trend line.
- `cor(..., method = "spearman")` calculates Spearman's rho.
- `mtext()` displays the rho value above the plot.

**Before knitting:** Make sure `CD_data_microbiom_essential.csv` is in the same folder as this `.Rmd` file, or set the RStudio working directory to the folder containing the CSV.
